claim_1.claim: CyTOF analysis of PBMCs from 52 COVID-19 patients and 62 healthy controls showed increased plasmablast and effector CD8 T cell frequencies and significantly reduced plasmacytoid dendritic cell frequencies in SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals compared to healthy controls.

sources.quote: There was a notable increase in the frequency of plasmablast and effector CD8 T cells in all infected individuals (Fig. 1B) in both cohorts
notably the frequency of plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) was significantly reduced in the PBMCs of SARS-CoV-2–infected individuals in both cohorts (Fig. 1C).

claim_2.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of ex vivo stimulated PBMCs from Atlanta cohort healthy and infected donors showed reduced pDC production of IFN-α and TNF-α and reduced mDC and CD14+ monocyte cytokine responses to viral and bacterial TLR ligands in infected individuals compared to healthy controls.

sources.quote: there was reduced production of IFN-α in response to the TLR stimuli in the pDCs of infected individuals compared with those of healthy controls (Fig. 2A). The TNF-α response was also significantly reduced in the pDCs of infected individuals

Notably, the response in mDCs as well as that in monocytes were also significantly lower in response to stimulation with a bacterial ligand cocktail (composed of TLR2, TLR4, and TLR5 ligands) or with the viral TLR cocktail (Fig. 2B and fig. S5).

claim_3.claim: Olink analysis of plasma from the Atlanta cohort showed that 43 cytokines were significantly up-regulated in COVID-19 infection, including IL-6, MCP-3, and CXCL10, and that TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and OSM were significantly increased in severe and ICU COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls.

sources.quote: Of the 92 analytes measured, 71 proteins were detected within the dynamic range of the assay. Of these 71 proteins, 43 cytokines, including IL-6, MCP-3, and CXCL10, were significantly up-regulated in COVID-19 infection

we identified three proteins that were significantly enhanced in COVID-19 infection and strongly correlated with clinical severity (Fig. 3, bottom row). These were TNFSF14 (LIGHT), EN-RAGE [S100A12, a biomarker of pulmonary injury that is implicated in the pathogenesis of sepsis-induced ARDS (21)], and oncostatin M [(OSM), a regulator of IL-6].

claim_4.claim: ELISA analysis of plasma showed a significant increase of TNFSF14, EN-RAGE, and OSM in severe and intensive care unit COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls, consistent with the multiplex Olink analysis.

sources.quote: we used an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to independently validate these results. Consistent with the multiplex Olink analysis, we found a significant increase of these inflammatory mediators in the plasma of severe and intensive care unit (ICU) COVID-19 patients.

claim_5.claim: CITE-seq analysis of PBMCs from 7 COVID-19 patients and 5 healthy controls showed emergence of interferon response-enriched T cell and monocyte clusters in COVID-19 samples, enhanced ISG expression despite little or no detectable IFN-α or IFN-β gene expression, reduced HLA-DR expression in myeloid cells, and increased S100A12 expression restricted to monocyte clusters compared to healthy controls.

sources.quote: Notably, we detected clusters of T cells and monocytes that were characterized by the expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as IFI27, IFITM3, or ISG15 (see C1-MONO_IFN and C18-T_IFN in fig. S10). These IFN response–enriched clusters emerged only in samples from COVID-19 patients
However, there was an enhanced expression of ISGs in patients with COVID-19 (Fig. 4D) in spite of an impaired capacity of the innate cells in the blood compartment to produce these cytokines.
we observed a reduction in the expression of the proteins CD86 and human leukocyte antigen class DR (HLA-DR) on monocytes and mDCs of COVID-19 patients

By contrast, S100A12, the gene encoding EN-RAGE, was substantially increased in the PBMCs of COVID-19 patients, whereas the expression of genes encoding other proinflammatory cytokines was either absent or unchanged compared with healthy controls (Fig. 5C and fig. S16B). Notably, the S100A12 expression was highly restricted to monocyte clusters (Fig. 5D)

claim_6.claim: ELISA analysis of plasma from 18 healthy and 40 COVID-19-infected patients showed that circulating IFN-α increased early after symptom onset, peaked around day 8 after onset of symptoms, and regressed to baseline levels by day 20.

sources.quote: We thus measured the concentration of IFN-α in plasma using a highly sensitive ELISA enabled by single molecule array (SIMoA) technology. We observed a marked increase in the concentration of IFN-α, which peaked around day 8 after onset of symptoms and regressed to baseline levels by day 20 (Fig. 4E).

claim_7.claim: Bulk RNA-seq analysis of total PBMCs from 17 COVID-19 patients and 17 healthy controls showed strong induction of a 33-gene ISG signature in COVID-19 subjects, no detectable expression of genes encoding IFN-α or IFN-β, reduced HLA-DR expression in monocytes and mDCs in severe disease, increased S100A12, and decreased TNF and TNFSF14 expression compared to healthy donors.

sources.quote: We observed a strong induction of the ISGs in COVID-19 subjects compared with healthy donors in this dataset as well (Fig. 4G). Of note, we did not detect expression of genes encoding IFN-α or IFN-β
Using the phospho-CyTOF data from both the Atlanta and Hong Kong cohorts, we confirmed the reduced expression of HLA-DR on monocytes and mDCs in patients with severe COVID-19 disease (Fig. 5B).

claim_8.claim: Q-PCR analysis of plasma from 18 healthy and 51 infected individuals showed significantly higher bacterial 16S rRNA gene copies in severe/ICU COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls.

sources.quote: the plasma of severe and ICU patients had significantly higher levels of bacterial DNA, as measured by PCR quantitation of bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene product

claim_9.claim: LPS reporter assay analysis of plasma from 18 healthy and 51 infected individuals showed significantly higher LPS levels in severe/ICU COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls.

sources.quote: the plasma of severe and ICU patients had significantly higher levels of bacterial DNA, as measured by PCR quantitation of bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene product, and of LPS, as measured by a TLR4-based reporter assay (Fig. 6, A and B).

claim_10.claim: Correlation analysis of plasma from 18 healthy and 51 infected individuals showed that bacterial DNA levels were significantly positively correlated with plasma IL-6, TNF, MCP-3, EN-RAGE, OSM, and TNFSF14.

sources.quote: Furthermore, there was a significant correlation between bacterial DNA or LPS and the plasma levels of the inflammatory mediators IL-6, TNF, MCP-3, EN-RAGE, TNFSF14, and OSM (Fig. 6C and fig. S19).
